title: How to plan the W Trek in Torres del Paine
lead: Park tickets, mandatory refugio and campsite bookings, which way to walk, how many days, when to go and how to reach Puerto Natales: a step-by-step plan for Patagonia's most famous multi-day hike, checked against CONAF and the park's official operators.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The W Trek is named for the shape it traces across the southern side of the Paine massif in Chilean Patagonia. It links the granite towers at Base Torres, the valley below Los Cuernos and Glacier Grey. The scenery gets the attention, but most of the work is in the planning. The trek is managed by CONAF, Chile's national forest service, and you can't just turn up with a tent. Here is the order we'd plan it in.
Step 1: Book your beds or tent sites first

This is the rule that catches most first-timers. CONAF says that to hike the W or the full Paine massif circuit (the O), you must book your overnight stays in advance. Without them you can't go into the mountain sector. The rule doesn't apply to day hikes such as Base Torres, to day trips along the road, or to the roadside campgrounds such as Camping Serrano and Camping Pehoé.

The refugios and campsites along the trail are run by two private operators, not by CONAF, and you book each one directly. Las Torres Patagonia (lastorres.com) runs the eastern and central sites, toward the towers and Los Cuernos. Vértice Patagonia (vertice.travel) runs Refugio & Camping Paine Grande, Refugio & Camping Grey, Refugio & Camping Dickson and Camping Los Perros. The last two are on the O circuit. Work out your nights first. Then book every stop before you buy flights, because each night has to line up with the next day's hike.

If you'd rather not piece it together yourself, Las Torres also sells a packaged W. It runs 5 days and 4 nights, or 4 days and 3 nights, with lodging, meals, park transport, the park entry ticket and the Lake Pehoé catamaran included. Its 2026–27 W departures run from October 2026 through April 2027.
Step 2: Buy your park entry ticket

Entry tickets are sold online through Pases Parques (pasesparques.cl), CONAF's official ticket portal. Your park ticket doesn't include a bed or a campsite. Those are booked separately (see Step 1). CONAF sells a day ticket and a multi-day ticket. For 2026 it lists the multi-day ticket for foreign adults at CLP 48,500. Children under 12, adults over 60 and people with disabilities get in free. Buy the ticket that matches the dates you booked.

CONAF lists park hours of 8:00 to 19:00, and hiking after dark is not allowed. For Base Torres, the 2026 schedule says you must start by 09:00 and be back down by 15:00. Times can change by season, so check the current schedule on the park's official site before you set your daily start times.
See Torres del Paine on the map, read our park overview and find more hikes in South America.
Step 3: Choose a direction and how many days

The W has two ends. The eastern end is the Torres sector, below the towers. The western end is Paine Grande, on Lake Pehoé, and from there a spur leads up to Glacier Grey. Paine Grande connects to the road by catamaran between Paine Grande and Pudeto. There is also a boat on Lake Grey. The Las Torres package walks east to west. It starts with a regular bus from Puerto Natales and ends with the Pehoé catamaran back toward town. Many hikers do the reverse. Choose a direction by what you can book: the order of your refugio or campsite nights decides it.

Las Torres sells the W in 4-day and 5-day versions. In our view, the extra day is worth it. It gives you room for a slower climb to the towers, and a spare half day if the weather turns. CONAF's daily trail report lists each W section as open or closed, along with any one-way-only stretches. Most one-way stretches are on the O, but check the report before you go.
Step 4: Pick your season, and respect the wind

The W is mainly a spring-to-autumn trip. Winter rules change things a lot. Under CONAF's 2026 winter rules, the W was open only with an accredited guide in May and August. It was closed completely in June and July. CONAF later kept the guide requirement through September 15 because of weather and trail conditions. From September 16, 2026, you no longer need a guide on the W or Base Torres. Microspikes and trekking poles may still be recommended or required while snow and ice remain. The O circuit stays closed through the winter, so check its reopening date with CONAF before planning a longer loop.

Patagonian weather changes fast, and CONAF can restrict or close trails when the forecast is bad. Its winter rules mention whiteout conditions on exposed passes. CONAF's advice is to check the forecast again and again while you're in the park. Pack a waterproof jacket and warm layers in every season. Keep your pack light enough to carry steadily in strong gusts. Allow some slack in your schedule, since a stormy day can mean waiting it out rather than pushing on.
Book the nights, then the ticket, then the flights, and leave room in the plan for Patagonia's weather.
Step 5: Getting to Puerto Natales and the park

Puerto Natales is the town where most W trips start and end. CONAF describes the route as a 250-kilometer paved road from Punta Arenas to Puerto Natales. From Puerto Natales you can reach the park on Route 9 North (about 150 km) or on the shorter Y-290 "Lago Porteño" road (about 80 km). The main entrances are Laguna Amarga, Sarmiento and Río Serrano.

CONAF's park page says regular buses leave Puerto Natales in the morning and the afternoon. Confirm the current timetable with the bus companies, and make sure your bus reaches the park in time for your first day's hike and your first night's booking. If your route uses the Pehoé catamaran, plan your return around its schedule.
Before you go

Stay on marked trails only. Lighting any fire or heat source outside permitted areas is banned and can bring heavy fines or prison time. Only approved camp stoves may be used, and only in designated areas. Pack out everything you bring in. If you want to see more of Patagonia after the W, Los Glaciares National Park, across the border in Argentina, makes a good second stop.
Continue to Los Glaciares, home of Fitz Roy and the Perito Moreno Glacier.

Rules, fees, trail status and seasonal closures in Torres del Paine change often, sometimes within a season. Always check current conditions and regulations with CONAF at parquetorresdelpaine.cl and conaf.cl, and confirm your bookings directly with the operators before you travel.

title: Walking the Milford Track: a complete guide
lead: Four days, three huts and one direction through the heart of Fiordland: how bookings, transport, huts and weather work on New Zealand's most famous Great Walk, straight from the Department of Conservation.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Milford Track runs from the head of Lake Te Anau to Sandfly Point on Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, through Fiordland National Park on New Zealand's South Island. The Department of Conservation (DOC) lists it as a 54 km (about 33.5 mile) walk over four days and three nights. It follows glacier-carved valleys and ancient beech forest, climbs over an alpine pass and passes some of the country's most famous waterfalls.

It is also one of the most tightly managed walks in the world. You can't drive to either end, you can't camp, and you can only walk it one way. Here's how it all fits together, with the details as DOC publishes them.
Season and bookings

The Great Walks season for 2026/27 runs from 1 November 2026 to 30 April 2027, with the last departure on 28 April 2027. During the season you must book all three huts in advance through the DOC booking system. Bookings for 2026/27 opened on 13 May 2026, and DOC says they are open now. Milford dates are in high demand, so check availability early and have backup dates ready.

DOC's own booking tips are simple: create your DOC booking account well before you need it, test your login before an opening day, read the rules for your track, and have a plan B if your first choice is full.

Hut fees are charged per person, per night. For the 2026/27 Great Walks season DOC lists NZ$106 for New Zealand adults and NZ$152 for international adults. Children pay NZ$53 (New Zealand, ages 5–17) or NZ$76 (international, ages 0–17), and New Zealand infants (0–4) stay free. Outside the season, the fee drops to NZ$30 per adult and NZ$15 per child. Fees change, so confirm them when you book.
One direction, three huts, no camping

The Milford Track can only be walked one way, from Glade Wharf to Sandfly Point. Camping is not permitted. Walkers stay in three DOC huts in order: Clinton Hut, then Mintaro Hut, then Dumpling Hut. For safety, DOC requires you to stay in each hut on the night shown on your booking confirmation.

Each hut has 40 bunks with mattresses in shared rooms. In the Great Walks season they have heating, toilets, basic cooking facilities with fuel, solar lighting and cold running water, and a DOC ranger lives on site. There are no showers and no cooking utensils, so bring your own pots, plates and cutlery. Outside the season, gas is not provided and the running water is turned off, so you need your own stove.
Explore Fiordland National Park on the map and see photos of Milford Sound from our community.
Getting there from Te Anau

There is no vehicle or private access to either end of the track, so you must book your transport in advance. From Te Anau, take a bus or private transport to Te Anau Downs (about 30 minutes). From there, a boat takes you to Glade Wharf at the head of Lake Te Anau (1 hour 15 minutes). At the end, a 20-minute boat ride runs from Sandfly Point to Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, where bus services connect back to Te Anau and on to Queenstown. DOC also points to guided walks on the track if you'd rather not go independently.
The track, day by day

Day 1: Glade Wharf to Clinton Hut, 5 km (about 3 miles), 1 to 1.5 hours. After the boat cruise, it's an easy walk through beech forest beside the Clinton River. DOC notes a short Wetland Walkway near the hut, about 15 minutes return.

Day 2: Clinton Hut to Mintaro Hut, 17.5 km (about 11 miles), about 6 hours. A gradual climb follows the Clinton River to its source at Lake Mintaro, at the foot of Omanui/McKinnon Pass. On the way you pass Hirere Falls and get views of the Pompolona icefield.

Day 3: Mintaro Hut to Dumpling Hut, 13 km (about 8 miles), 6 to 7 hours. This is the big day. You climb to Omanui/McKinnon Pass, the highest point of the track at 1,154 m (about 3,786 feet), then descend around 1,000 m through alpine gardens and past waterfalls along the Roaring Burn. DOC calls the side trip to Sutherland Falls a definite highlight. It takes about 1 hour 30 minutes return, and the falls drop 580 m (about 1,900 feet) in three leaps from Lake Quill.

Day 4: Dumpling Hut to Sandfly Point, 18 km (about 11 miles), 5.5 to 6 hours. You follow the Arthur River past the historic Boatshed, Mackay Falls and Bell Rock. The last 3 km is a smooth, wide track built by a prison labour gang between 1890 and 1892, ending at the boat to Milford Sound.
Book the huts and both boats before anything else, then pack for rain, whatever month it is.
Weather and safety

Fiordland is one of the wettest places in New Zealand. DOC notes rainfall of up to 9,000 mm (about 354 inches) a year, and warns that cold temperatures, snow, strong winds and heavy rain can happen at any time of year. Both the Clinton and Arthur valleys become impassable in heavy rain. Pack a good waterproof jacket and warm layers even in midsummer, and keep your gear dry in a pack liner. There is no cellphone coverage on the track.

Avalanche risk can extend into December, and DOC counts more than 57 avalanche paths along the route. Outside the Great Walks season (May to late October), the track is not managed. DOC says it should only be attempted by fit, experienced and well-equipped people, with alpine gear such as an ice axe and crampons, plus an avalanche beacon, snow shovel and probe. DOC also does not recommend the track for children under 10, because of the exposed mountain terrain and frequent bad weather.
More Great Walks

If Milford dates are full, or you'd like a gentler coastal walk, the Abel Tasman Coast Track at the top of the South Island is another DOC Great Walk. Note that its huts and campsites must be booked in advance all year round.
See Abel Tasman National Park, with golden beaches and coastal forest at the top of the South Island.
Track conditions, closures, fees and transport change often. Always check current track alerts, weather and regulations with the Department of Conservation at doc.govt.nz/milfordtrack before you go.

title: Inca Trail permits, and the best alternatives if they're sold out
lead: How Inca Trail permits really work, why the trail closes every February, how Machu Picchu tickets and circuits fit in, and what to hike instead if the dates you want are gone. Rules straight from Peru's Ministry of Culture and SERNANP.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Walking the Inca Trail to Machu Picchu is on almost every hiker's list, and it's also one of the most tightly managed treks in the world. The trail runs through the Historic Sanctuary of Machupicchu, which is co-managed by Peru's Ministry of Culture and SERNANP, the national protected areas service. Below is how access works, what to book, and the official alternatives if the permits for your dates are gone.
How Inca Trail permits work

You can't buy an Inca Trail permit yourself. SERNANP says entry to the Inca Trail Network is only through travel and tourism agencies authorized by the sanctuary, and it publishes the list of authorized operators on its visitor page. Your operator reserves the permit in your name through the Ministry of Culture's electronic booking system, so pick a company from that list and book through it.

The network is made up of several numbered routes. Route 1, the classic trail, starts at Piskacucho (km 82), and SERNANP recommends 4 days and 3 nights for it. Route 2 starts at Qoriwayrachina (km 88), and Route 4 starts at km 82 and follows the valley floor via Chachabamba in 3 days and 2 nights. Route 5 is the one-day option (more on that below).

Spaces are limited and the booking window opens early. In past years, the Cusco office of the Ministry of Culture (DDC Cusco) opened reservations for the following season in October, month by month. If you have fixed dates, talk to an authorized operator as early as you can, and ask what is included: the trail permit, the guide, and your Machu Picchu entry.
The February closure

The Inca Trail Network closes every February. DDC Cusco uses the month for maintenance and conservation, including clearing vegetation from archaeological sites, consolidating paving and stone stairways, repairing bridges and handrails, and rehabilitating campsites. In 2026 the trail reopened on March 1. February also falls inside the rainy season, which SERNANP lists as November to March. The sanctuary recommends visiting from April to October.

Rain can close the trail at other times as well. On August 18, 2026, unusually heavy rain caused landslides and flooded campsites, and the Ministry of Culture suspended access to the network. Routes 1, 2 and 3 reopened on August 26, and Route 5 stayed open as an alternative. Build a little flexibility into your plans.
See Machu Picchu on the map, with trip facts, best season and our Classic Inca Trail overview.
Machu Picchu tickets, circuits and rules

Entry to the Inca city itself (the llaqta) is ticketed separately by the Ministry of Culture. Since June 1, 2024 the site has had three circuits containing ten routes. Circuit 1 (Panoramic) includes the Machupicchu Mountain route. Circuit 2 (Classic) covers the designed route through the city and the lower terrace route. Circuit 3 (Royalty) includes the Waynapicchu (Huayna Picchu) route. Some routes, such as the Intipunku (Sun Gate) and Inca Bridge routes, run only in high season. Each ticket is tied to a circuit, a route and an entry time.

Buy tickets online at tuboleto.cultura.pe, the official state platform. You'll need an account registered with your passport and an email address. The ministry also sells up to 1,000 tickets a day in person at its office in Machupicchu Pueblo, valid for entry the next day, and you can check how many are left in real time on the same platform. Bring the passport you booked with, because staff check that your ID and entry time match your ticket.
A few site rules matter for hikers. Bags larger than 40 × 35 × 20 cm (16 × 14 × 8 in) aren't allowed, and neither are walking sticks, food, or drones. Stay on your assigned circuit and route.
Acclimatise before you hike

Most treks start from Cusco, which the CDC lists at about 11,000 feet (roughly 3,350 m), well above the 8,000 ft (2,450 m) level where unacclimatized travelers become at risk of altitude illness. The CDC's travel guidance notes that for Cusco, travelers can first sleep for 1 to 2 nights at elevations lower than the airport before heading up. It also points out that 2 to 3 nights at moderate altitude before going higher strongly protects against acute mountain sickness.

Headache is the main symptom, often with nausea, dizziness, fatigue or loss of appetite. The CDC's rule is simple: never go higher to sleep while you have symptoms, and go down if they get worse. Talk to your doctor before the trip about whether preventive medication makes sense for you.
If permits are sold out: the one-day short Inca Trail

Route 5 is the short Inca Trail. You take the train to Chachabamba (km 104) and walk past Wiñaywayna and through Intipunku, the Sun Gate, to Machu Picchu. SERNANP lists it at 10.5 km, with a recommended time of one day. It's still part of the Inca Trail Network, so it also has to be booked through an authorized operator. Book it as early as the classic route rather than as a last-minute backup.

Route 5 has had a disrupted year. After a geological event at Chachabamba on March 31, 2026, the Ministry of Culture closed the km 104 access and routed hikers in from km 106 (Choquesuysuy) instead. SERNANP announced that the Chachabamba–Wiñaywayna section would reopen on August 1, 2026. In late August the ministry listed entry to Route 5 via both km 104 and km 106. Confirm the current starting point with your operator.
The Salkantay alternative

Salkantay is the big glaciated peak southwest of Machu Picchu, and the treks around it are the best-known alternative to the classic trail. Peru's official tourism board describes a 5-day, 4-night trek from Mollepata, about two hours by road from Cusco, and says hiring a guide is mandatory. Expect real altitude and cold nights. The board gives lows around 1 °C (34 °F).

Be aware that some Salkantay itineraries enter the Inca Trail Network. SERNANP's Route 3 starts at Soraypampa, crosses below Salkantay and joins the classic trail at Wayllabamba (42.1 km, 5 days and 4 nights). That route needs an Inca Trail permit like any other. Treks that don't use the network still finish at the llaqta, so you'll need your own Machu Picchu ticket. Ask your operator which kind you're booking.
Book the permit early, acclimatise in Cusco, and keep a backup plan. Machu Picchu is worth it whichever way you arrive.
Before you go

Rules, routes and closures in the sanctuary change, sometimes at short notice after rain or landslides. Always check current conditions and regulations with Peru's Ministry of Culture (machupicchu.gob.pe and DDC Cusco) and SERNANP before you travel, and confirm every booking detail with your authorized operator.

title: Your first multi-day trek: what to pack and how to prepare
lead: Going from day hikes to sleeping on the trail is a big step. Here is how to pack by category, dress in layers, handle water and food, find your way and leave no trace, based on guidance from park authorities, the CDC and Leave No Trace.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: A multi-day trek changes the math of hiking. You carry your bed, your kitchen and every meal, and you can't turn back to the car when the weather changes. The good news is that park authorities publish clear gear lists and safety rules. We pulled together the advice from the US National Park Service, New Zealand's Department of Conservation (DOC), Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service, Chile's CONAF and the Leave No Trace Center so your first trek starts on the right foot.
Start with the Ten Essentials

The National Park Service describes the Ten Essentials as items that help you handle minor injuries, sudden weather changes or unexpected emergencies. They are: navigation (map, compass and GPS), sun protection (sunglasses, sunscreen and a hat), extra clothing, illumination (a headlamp is the hands-free choice), first-aid supplies, fire (matches or a lighter and fire starters), a repair kit and tools, nutrition (a day's worth of extra food), hydration (water plus a way to treat it) and emergency shelter. On a multi-day trek most of these are already in your pack. The point is to check that none are missing.
Packing by category

Pack and shelter. DOC's multi-day gear list suggests a 40–60 litre backpack with a waterproof or plastic pack liner to keep your gear dry. Add a 3–4 season sleeping bag. If you're staying in huts, check what they provide. DOC's Great Walk huts have bunks and mattresses but no bedding, and on the Abel Tasman Coast Track the huts have no gas for cooking or lighting. If you're camping, you'll need a tent and sleeping mat too.

Kitchen. Bring a stove and fuel, a lighter or waterproof matches, a pot, utensils and a cup. DOC reminds walkers that you can't buy food on the track. Check each track's rules too. In Torres del Paine, CONAF prohibits lighting fires and only allows stoves that don't burn plant material.

Safety kit. Pack a first-aid kit with blister care, a headlamp with spare batteries, and a survival kit. DOC's version includes a survival blanket, whistle, paper, pencil and high-energy snacks. Carry a distress beacon. DOC lists one on its gear list, and Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service notes that many Overland Track walkers carry a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB), which you can hire locally.
Fiordland's Great Walks are a classic first hut-to-hut trek. See the park on our map.
Dress in layers, and skip the cotton

Mountain weather changes fast, so build a system you can add to or take off: a wool or synthetic base layer, a fleece or wool mid-layer, and a waterproof, windproof jacket with a hood plus overtrousers. Add a warm hat, gloves, a sunhat and sunglasses. DOC is blunt about cotton. Jeans, T-shirts and sweatshirts won't keep you warm when they're wet. Wear wool or synthetic socks and well broken-in boots.

DOC also suggests one set of clothes to walk in and a separate dry set for camp and sleeping, since hut bunkrooms aren't heated and you can't count on drying your gear there. Tasmania's park service puts it starkly: deaths have occurred on the Overland Track when people were caught unprepared in cold, wet and windy weather.
The Overland Track crosses alpine country where warm, waterproof layers are a must. Explore Cradle Mountain–Lake St Clair.
Water: carry it, then treat it

Don't assume stream or hut water is safe. On the Abel Tasman Coast Track, DOC says hut and campsite water is untreated and should be boiled before use. The CDC calls boiling the best way to kill germs: bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet. The next best option is to filter and then disinfect. A filter with a pore size of 0.3 micron or smaller removes bacteria and parasites but not viruses. Chlorine and iodine kill bacteria and viruses but don't work well on parasites. Chlorine dioxide tablets can kill Giardia. If you use chemicals, follow the product's waiting time.
Food: plan every meal, plus a spare day

Plan each breakfast, lunch, dinner and snack for the number of nights you'll be out, and choose light, energy-dense food. Then add extra. The NPS suggests an extra day's supply of no-cook, nutrient-dense food, such as trail mix or granola bars. DOC says to carry emergency food in case weather delays you. Leave No Trace also recommends repackaging food at home to cut down on trash, which you'll carry out anyway.
Navigation and planning

Carry a paper map and compass even if you use a GPS or phone app. The NPS recommends physical maps as a backup, and both DOC and Tasmania's park service list a map and compass. Study the route before you go. Some tracks have hazards that depend on timing. On the Abel Tasman Coast Track, the Awaroa Inlet can only be crossed within 1 hour 30 minutes before and 2 hours after low tide, and only in daylight. Torres del Paine prohibits hiking without daylight and only allows travel on authorized trails marked on the official map.
Book ahead where it's required. Abel Tasman huts and campsites must be booked in advance year round, and in Torres del Paine CONAF strictly prohibits overnight stays outside authorized areas.
Golden beaches, tidal crossings and bookable huts: see Abel Tasman on our map.
Leave No Trace on overnight trips

Leave No Trace's seven principles are: plan ahead and prepare, travel and camp on durable surfaces, dispose of waste properly, leave what you find, minimize campfire impacts, respect wildlife, and be considerate of other visitors. They matter most when you sleep out. Camp at least 200 feet from lakes and streams. Where there's no toilet, dig catholes 6 to 8 inches deep, at least 200 feet from water, camp and trails. Carry wash water 200 feet away from streams or lakes. Use a stove instead of a fire, and never feed animals.
Torres del Paine has strict camping and fire rules. Explore the park on our map.
Pack for the worst day you could have on the trail, not the best one.
Safety before you set out

Tell someone your plans and when you expect to be back, as DOC's Land Safety Code advises. For a first trek, choose a well-marked route with huts or set campsites, and keep your daily distances modest. Walk with company. CONAF tells Torres del Paine visitors to hike accompanied. Check the weather forecast often, and be ready to wait out a storm rather than push through it.

Track conditions, booking rules, fire bans and seasonal requirements change. Always check current conditions and regulations with the park authority before you go: DOC for New Zealand, Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service, CONAF for Torres del Paine, or the National Park Service in the US.

title: The best day hikes in Yosemite
lead: Waterfall stairways, a quiet lake, granite viewpoints and the most famous permit in the park: six classic Yosemite day hikes, with the numbers and rules straight from the National Park Service.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Yosemite packs an unusual amount of drama into short distances. From the floor of Yosemite Valley you can climb beside thundering falls in a morning, and from the rim along Glacier Point Road you can reach huge viewpoints in about an hour. Below are the day hikes we think every first visit should consider, with distances and elevation gain as the National Park Service lists them.

Good news for 2026: the park announced it will not use a timed entry reservation system this year. Instead it is managing traffic and parking in real time, and it encourages weekday visits. Popular trailheads still fill early, so plan to start your day early or use the free Valley shuttles.
1. Mist Trail to Vernal and Nevada Falls

This is Yosemite's signature waterfall hike. It starts at Happy Isles (shuttle stop #16). You can turn around at the Vernal Fall footbridge (1.6 miles round trip, 400 feet of gain, moderate) or continue up the Mist Trail's steep granite stairway to the top of Vernal Fall (2.4 miles round trip, 1,000 feet of gain, strenuous, about 3 hours). Strong hikers can keep going to the top of Nevada Fall (5.4 miles round trip via the Mist Trail, 2,000 feet of gain, 5–6 hours).

In spring and early summer the spray soaks the steps, which can be slick, so wear shoes with good grip and a light rain layer. Drinking water is available at the trailhead and at the Vernal Fall footbridge from May to October. The lower Mist Trail closes in winter because of falling ice and rock; the John Muir Trail is the alternate route to the top of Vernal Fall.

Heads-up for this fall: through October (subject to change), the section of the Mist Trail from the John Muir Trail junction to the top of Vernal Fall is only open Fridays through Sundays and on holidays because of repair work.
2. Upper Yosemite Fall

One of the oldest trails in the park, and one of the toughest day hikes in the Valley. It begins near Camp 4 (shuttle stop #7). Columbia Rock makes a good shorter goal at 2 miles round trip and 2–3 hours. The full climb to the top of Yosemite Falls is 7.2 miles round trip with 2,700 feet of gain and takes 6–8 hours.

Start early: the NPS warns this trail gets very hot at midday in summer, and the upper section has no shade until late afternoon. There is no drinking water along the trail, and the park suggests carrying about 4 quarts (liters) for the full hike. Stay on the trail; there are steep drop-offs and ledges off-trail. Go in spring for the biggest flow. By August the fall may be only a trickle, and in winter the upper trail can be icy or buried in snow.
See Yosemite on the map, read our park overview and find more hikes in North America.
3. Mirror Lake

An easy-to-moderate walk below Half Dome, and a good choice for families or a rest day. It starts at shuttle stop #17. The out-and-back to the lake is 2 miles with about 100 feet of gain and takes about an hour. The full 5-mile loop takes 2–3 hours. The lake is fullest in spring and early summer, when Tenaya Creek runs with snowmelt. By late summer it turns into what the park calls Mirror Meadow. The trail is open all year, but sections can be icy in winter.
4. Sentinel Dome and 5. Taft Point

These two short hikes share the Sentinel Dome/Taft Point Trailhead on Glacier Point Road, and they deliver some of the biggest views in the park for very little effort. Sentinel Dome is 2 miles round trip with 400 feet of gain (1–2 hours) and ends with a walk up open granite to a 360-degree view. Taft Point is 2.2 miles round trip with about 200 feet of gain on the way back (1–2 hours) and ends at a sheer viewpoint on the rim of Yosemite Valley.

Glacier Point Road is usually open from May to November, depending on conditions. Stay off the domes during thunderstorms, and bring all the water you need, since there's little available out there. At the time of writing in early October 2026, the road was temporarily closed because of smoke and firefighting operations from the Dome Fire, with no estimated reopening date. Check before you drive up.
6. Half Dome: the permit lottery

Half Dome is the bucket-list day hike: 14 to 16 miles round trip, about 4,800 feet of gain, and 10 to 12 hours for most hikers, ending with the cables up the final granite slope. While the cables are up, roughly from the Friday before Memorial Day until mid-October, you need a permit to go to the top.

Most permits go out in a preseason lottery on Recreation.gov. You apply March 1–31, and results arrive in mid-April. During the season, a daily lottery opens two days before the hike date for any remaining permits. There is a $10 non-refundable application fee, plus $10 per person if you win. The park says nearly all fatal falls from the cables have happened when the rock was wet, so don't go up in wet conditions. Set a firm turnaround time, and stay off the summit when storms build.
Pick your hike by season: waterfalls in spring, the high rim roads in summer and early fall, and always an early start.
Staying safe on Yosemite trails

Rivers and waterfalls cause many of the park's emergencies. Do not swim or wade above waterfalls or in fast water near the Mist Trail, because the current can be deadly. Carry plenty of water (the park suggests at least 1 quart every 2 hours), a headlamp even on short hikes, and sturdy shoes with good traction. Tell someone your plan and when you expect to be back.
Yosemite is black bear country. Store all food in bear-proof lockers or containers, since bears will break into cars for food, and stay at least 50 yards from any bear you see on the trail.
Trail closures, road status, waterfall flow and fire conditions change often. Always check current conditions and regulations with the National Park Service at nps.gov/yose before you go.

title: Planning the W Trek in Torres del Paine
lead: Granite towers, glacier lakes and Patagonian wind: how to shape the park's classic multi-day route around your days and your style.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The W Trek takes its name from the shape it traces on the map: three valleys walked one after another along the southern side of the Paine massif. Most hikers spend four to five days on it, sleeping in refugios or campsites along the way.
When to go
The main season runs through the southern summer, roughly October to April. Expect long days, quickly changing weather and strong wind at any time of year — pack layers rather than one heavy jacket.
Read the park overview, see it on the map and find more hikes in South America.
Book before you fly
Campsites and refugios on the route must be reserved in advance, and they fill up early in peak season. Plan the order of your nights first, then build the rest of the trip around them.
Start early for the towers: the last climb is steep, and morning light on the granite is worth the alarm.
Always check current conditions and regulations with the park authority before you go — routes and booking rules change.

title: Five waterfall hikes for your bucket list
lead: From thundering curtains of water to turquoise terraces: five trails where the destination is a splash.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Waterfalls reward even short walks with a big finale. These five, spread across four continents, are on our list for their scale, their colour and the trails that lead to them.
Walkways bring you right to the edge of one of the largest waterfall systems on Earth.
Boardwalks thread between terraced lakes in impossible shades of green and blue.
Limestone pools step down through the forest outside Luang Prabang.
Granite walls and long falls that peak with the spring snowmelt.
A valley of colourful lakes and cascades in the Sichuan mountains.
